attribution.note: Marcus's own words on his Substack. He republishes them with a disclosure that they were reused from his 2022 essay, so he still endorses them.

semantics.note: 'Will' within a decade is a firm forecast. The hedge 'maybe much less' applies only to the earlier timing, so the decade deadline still binds. The normalised claim keeps the scope and the horizon.

contract.note: The plain reading (a shift in the field's main emphasis) is ordinary and fair. Measuring the decade from 2025 or from the 2022 original gives 2035 or 2032. Neither date has passed, so the choice does not change today's result.

evidence.note: A 2026 Google Research blog post, which is a company disclosure. It points to growing agent work but does not measure a field-wide change in emphasis.
A systematic review of neuro-symbolic papers from 2020 to 2024. It covers the period before the forecast and gives no measure of the field's overall focus afterwards.

reviews.rationale: The deadline is 2035-07-27, which is after the evaluation date. The early-resolution rule needs convergent longitudinal evidence of a field-wide shift, and the packet has only illustrative items and pre-forecast context. The forecast cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction about GPT-5 in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Will remain difficult to anticipate' is a firm forecast. The normalised claim keeps the core but leaves out the companion part ('often do what you want, sometimes not'). That omission is minor.

contract.note: Reading the claim as users' difficulty predicting success in advance is an ordinary reading. Marcus gave no threshold or task set, and treating error rates as unpredictability would change the result. The contract rightly marks that.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own launch benchmarks, which are a company disclosure. They show successes and failures but do not test whether failures could be predicted in advance.
A 2026 benchmark on 40 cases that scores run-to-run output consistency. Consistency across repeated runs is not the same as users predicting which requests will succeed.

reviews.rationale: No item measures whether users can tell in advance which GPT-5 requests will succeed or fail across representative tasks. Accuracy and consistency scores are only indirect. With no deadline and no evaluation that settles the question, the claim stays unresolved.
